name: Raspberry Pi Holdings plc (and the Raspberry Pi Foundation)
origin_detail: The Raspberry Pi Foundation, a UK educational charity, was established in autumn 2008 to promote computer science in schools. It launched the $35 Model B on 29 Feb 2012. Its trading subsidiary was incorporated on 10 Sep 2012 as Newincco 1209 Ltd, took the name Raspberry Pi (Trading) Ltd on 18 Dec 2012 and was renamed Raspberry Pi Ltd in Nov 2021 (Companies House 08207441). It became part of Raspberry Pi Holdings plc, which listed on the London Stock Exchange in June 2024.
flagship_projects: Raspberry Pi single-board computers (Model B 2012 to Pi 5)
openness_notes: Hardware column. The single-board-computer designs and the Broadcom SoCs are closed. The official boot firmware is proprietary: its source is not public, but the binary may be freely redistributed. The OS is a Debian-based Linux distribution. At launch (Feb 2012) the VideoCore graphics userland was closed too, so only the peripheral software was open (level 1). Opening came in steps. The VideoCore IV userland driver was released as free software in Oct 2012, and the full graphics documentation and stack followed under BSD-3-Clause in Feb 2014. The microcontroller line opened further: the Pico SDK is BSD-3-Clause, and the RP2350's Hazard3 RISC-V cores are Apache-2.0. The current level is 2 (software and most firmware open, hardware designs closed). This is the 'open software, closed hardware' pattern.

exit_events.note: Listed 11 Jun 2024 at a 280p offer price, valuing the company at about GBP 541.6M. Converted at the 1.2723 USD/GBP implied by CNBC's GBP 166M = $211.2M. The offering raised about GBP 166M ($211.2M) and was made up of 45.9M existing shares sold by the Foundation's subsidiary Raspberry Pi Mid Co, 2.13M from other holders and 11.23M new shares. The shares closed day one up 38% at 388p.

risk_events: 2024: the IPO cut the Foundation's stake. It held 77.31% of Raspberry Pi Holdings before listing (prospectus) and 49.08% in the months after (Wikipedia text; the infobox says 41%).
2026-04: the Foundation agreed to sell 10.9M more shares (Halifax, cited by Wikipedia).

2026: an AI-driven global memory-chip shortage raised component costs. The company used debt facilities for strategic inventory and warned that first-half unit economics would moderate (Kalkine, 2026-11-02).
2026: share-price volatility. The 52-week range was 253.8-1,082p, with a record in June 2026, and the price was 469.4p on 2026-11-23.
Single-source dependencies: SoCs come from Broadcom and most manufacturing is outsourced to Sony.
The proprietary boot firmware means the platform cannot be fully rebuilt from source.
robustness: The company is listed and profitable (FY2025 net income $21.7M). The Foundation is still the largest holder, so the education mission keeps an anchor, but it is selling down. The installed base is very large: over 75M boards by March 2026, and 70% of 2024 sales went to industrial customers. The silicon is a single-vendor dependency: the closed Broadcom SoC and proprietary firmware mean no second source can rebuild the boards, and the open software stack is what keeps users' work portable.
physical_science_relevance: Pis are a standard low-cost controller for lab automation, data logging and camera streaming. This lab's CubXL controller is a Pi 5. Pico/RP2040 boards are common in DIY instruments, and the Pico SDK is permissively licensed.
openness_effect_assessment: Raspberry Pi shows that closed silicon and closed boards on top of an open software stack can scale: over 75M units by March 2026 and $323.2M revenue in 2025. Industrial buyers, who made up 70% of 2024 sales, are buying supply continuity rather than design openness. The step-by-step opening of the graphics stack (2012-2014), the BSD-licensed Pico SDK and the Apache-2.0 Hazard3 core grew the developer ecosystem without giving away the board designs. The sources read document no exact-copy clone problem of the kind Arduino reports.
key_takeaway: Raspberry Pi is the clearest success of 'open software, closed hardware' in this group. A charity founded it, it went public in 2024 at about $689M, and it was worth about $1.19B on 2026-11-23, profitable on hardware sales alone. Openness sits in the OS, drivers and microcontroller SDK. The SoC, boot firmware and board designs stay proprietary and single-sourced from Broadcom and Sony, which protects margins but leaves the platform dependent on one vendor. Foundation ownership locks in the mission but is being diluted by share sales. For the study it is the counterexample to the idea that the leading maker-hardware firms are open hardware: one of the most valuable firms in the space is not open hardware at all.
